guide.summary: Unit 1 builds the reading skills the whole course depends on: reading Latin prose at sight, recognizing forms quickly, and identifying the constructions AP tests most often, such as ablative absolutes, indirect statement, subjunctive clauses, and gerundives.

sections.heading: Reading strategy
sections.body: Read the whole sentence before translating. Find the main verb and its subject, then attach clauses and phrases. Latin word order is flexible, so endings, not position, show function. Group words that agree (noun–adjective, noun–participle) and bracket subordinate clauses introduced by cum, ut, ne, qui, quod, dum, or si. Context and vocabulary help, but every choice must fit the grammar.

sections.heading: Core constructions
sections.body: Ablative absolute: a noun and participle in the ablative, grammatically independent of the main clause (Nautis convocatis, 'after the sailors had been called together'). Indirect statement: a verb of saying or thinking plus accusative subject and infinitive (dixit merces iaciendas esse, 'he said that the goods had to be thrown'). Purpose and indirect command with ut/ne + subjunctive (oravit ut navem servarent). Result clauses after tantus, tam, ita, sic (tanta tempestas ut... desperarent). Cum clauses (circumstantial, causal, concessive) with the subjunctive. The passive periphrastic (gerundive + esse) expresses obligation. Place constructions: names of cities take the accusative without a preposition for motion toward (Athenas), the ablative for motion from, and the locative for location (Romae, Athenis).

sections.heading: Translating for the exam
sections.body: AP translation scoring checks that every word is accounted for and that tenses, voices, moods, and constructions are rendered literally. A pluperfect subjunctive in a cum clause becomes 'when he had loaded'; a future active infinitive in indirect statement becomes 'would perish' after a past verb. Natural English is welcome only when it keeps the grammar visible. In multiple choice on sight passages, test each answer against the endings; distractors often swap subject and object or misread tense.

sections.heading: Worked example: a complex sentence
sections.body: Consider the sentence Caesar, cum hostes fugere vidisset, milites hortatus est ut eos celeriter sequerentur. Start with the main clause: Caesar ... hortatus est, 'Caesar encouraged' (hortor is deponent, so the passive form has an active meaning). Next, bracket the cum clause: cum hostes fugere vidisset, 'when he had seen that the enemy were fleeing'. Inside it, vidisset introduces an indirect statement with hostes as the accusative subject and fugere as the infinitive. Finally, the ut clause is an indirect command after hortatus est: 'to follow them quickly'. Put together: 'When Caesar had seen that the enemy were fleeing, he encouraged the soldiers to follow them quickly.' Working clause by clause, and identifying each verb's mood and function, prevents the most common errors.

sections.heading: Forms that are easy to confuse
sections.body: Many endings look alike, so context matters. The ending -is can be dative or ablative plural in the first and second declensions, or genitive singular in the third. The ending -ae can be genitive or dative singular, or nominative plural. Third-declension neuter plurals end in -a, which can be mistaken for feminine singulars. Verb forms also overlap: amaris is present passive second person singular, while amaveris can be future perfect indicative or perfect subjunctive. Participles agree with nouns in gender, number, and case, which helps you find the noun they modify even when they are far apart in the sentence. Always check that your translation accounts for every ending.

sections.heading: Sight-reading practice routine
sections.body: Read a short passage aloud first to get a feel for its sentence breaks. Then underline every verb and note its tense, voice, and mood. Mark subordinate clauses with brackets and identify their type. Translate the main clauses first, then add the subordinate clauses, then check that every word fits. Keep a vocabulary list of frequent words you miss, and review principal parts of common irregular verbs such as sum, possum, eo, fero, volo, and fio.

sections.heading: Going deeper
sections.body: Participles are among the most tested forms. The present active participle (amans, amantis) shows action at the same time as the main verb; the perfect passive participle (amatus) shows action completed before it; the future active participle (amaturus) shows action yet to come. Gerunds are verbal nouns (amandi, 'of loving'), while gerundives are verbal adjectives (liber legendus, 'a book to be read'). Ad + gerund or gerundive and causa + genitive both express purpose. Supines in -um after verbs of motion also express purpose (venerunt spectatum, 'they came to watch'). Recognizing these forms quickly speeds sight reading and helps you translate literally on the free response.

keyTakeaways: Endings, not word order, show function.
ut/ne + subjunctive: purpose, result, indirect command.
City names: no preposition for place to/from.
commonMistakes: Translating an ablative absolute as the subject.
Missing the tense relationship of infinitives in indirect statement.
examTips: Check sequence of tenses for subjunctives.
Translate literally; don't smooth away grammar.
guide.cramSheet:
**Ablative absolute:** noun + participle (abl.) · **Indirect statement:** acc. + inf. · **Subjunctive:** purpose (ut/ne) · result (tantus…ut) · indirect command · cum clauses · indirect question

**Gerundive:** obligation (-ndus + esse) · **Place:** Athenas (to), Athenis (from/locative) · **Infinitives:** pres. (same time), perf. (before), fut. (after)

vocab.definition: Noun/pronoun + participle in the ablative, independent of the main clause.
Accusative subject + infinitive after verbs of saying, thinking, perceiving.
ut/ne + subjunctive after verbs of ordering or asking.
ut/ut non + subjunctive after tantus, tam, ita, sic.
cum + subjunctive meaning when, since, or although.
Case showing location for cities and small islands.
Rule matching subjunctive tense to the main verb's time.
Passive in form, active in meaning (e.g., sequor).

practice.stimulus:
**Sight passage** (Original Latin composed by Klutch for sight-reading practice.)

Mercator quidam, cum navem onerasset, Athenas navigare constituit. Nautis convocatis, "Ventis secundis," inquit, "celeriter perveniemus." Sed tertio die tanta tempestas orta est ut nautae de salute desperarent. Mercator, qui merces amittere nolebat, deos oravit ut navem servarent. Tum gubernator, vir prudens, dixit merces in mare iaciendas esse; aliter omnes perituros. Mercator invitus paruit, et navis, onere levata, in portum incolumis pervenit.

practice.prompt:
Translate the passage below as literally as possible.

Mercator, qui merces amittere nolebat, deos oravit ut navem servarent. Tum gubernator, vir prudens, dixit merces in mare iaciendas esse; aliter omnes perituros. Mercator invitus paruit, et navis, onere levata, in portum incolumis pervenit.

rubric.description: qui ... nolebat → who was unwilling / did not want
deos oravit → begged/prayed to the gods
ut navem servarent → to save the ship / that they save the ship
merces ... iaciendas esse → that the goods had to be thrown
aliter omnes perituros → otherwise all would perish
Mercator invitus paruit → the merchant unwillingly obeyed
onere levata → relieved of its load
in portum incolumis pervenit → arrived safe into the harbor

practice.sampleResponse: The merchant, who did not want to lose his goods, begged the gods to save the ship. Then the helmsman, a sensible man, said that the goods had to be thrown into the sea; otherwise all would perish. The merchant unwillingly obeyed, and the ship, relieved of its load, arrived safe in the harbor.
